title: Sequencing modules and how they relate
description: Connect sequencing and optical barcode workflows to phenotype scores, regression, experiment planning, power estimates, dose-response analysis and run comparison.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: Sequencing is how a pooled screen learns which guide sits in which well or cell, and spaCR reads it two ways. Reads from a sequencer go into Map Barcodes. Barcodes imaged cycle by cycle go into OPS, which lives inside Mask. Either way, the barcode identities end up beside your phenotypes in Regression. Around that core sit the planning tools, Experiment Design and Power, for before you acquire, and Dose–Response and Run Compare for your results.

Start with the sequencing reads. Open Map Barcodes from Home and give it your FASTQ files, single-end or paired, with the barcode reference tables that encode your experiment. Map Barcodes matches each read to its barcodes and counts the guides in every well, saving unique_combinations.csv and annotated_reads.h5 in its run folder. Before you trust those counts, open them in Barcode QC. Once they pass, they are the guide counts Regression pairs with phenotype scores, on the same plate and well keys.

Barcode QC lives inside Map Barcodes, so open Map Barcodes from Home and choose it there. It reads the guide counts you just made and shows mapping depth, coverage, barcode collisions and positional effects. It saves the QC results with exportable figures and tables, so you can decide which guides to filter before going further.

Optical screens take a different road. Open Mask from Home, then choose OPS. Instead of reads, OPS takes the images from each sequencing cycle, aligns them to the phenotype images and decodes a barcode for every nucleus. The results land in the OPS measurements.db, with tables for geometry, phenotype alignment, nuclei and barcodes. That database is not a FASTQ count table, though. To use it in Regression, first join and aggregate the decoded identities with your phenotype data, so each object or well carries both.

Whichever way you sequenced, barcodes meet phenotypes in Regression. Open it from Home. For a pooled screen, it takes phenotype scores from Classify and guide counts from Map Barcodes. For an optical screen, it takes the decoded OPS objects once you have joined and aggregated them yourself; that is not a direct file handoff. It can also model a directly measured response. In every case, plate and well identifiers must agree across the inputs. Choose the response and the controls, run the fit, and read the diagnostics before you call anything a hit. The results folder it writes, with coefficients, hit tables, settings and figures, is what Run Compare opens when you want to line this run up against another.

Now step back to before the experiment. Open Power / Design from Home to estimate how much sampling you need to see an effect, based on the effect sizes and variability you choose. Pilot measurements can support those assumptions, but they are optional. The layout from Experiment Design feeds these estimates, and the estimates in turn may send you back to revise that design.

Open Experiment Design from Home to lay out the plates before you acquire anything. Enter the conditions, controls, replicates and plate constraints, with your power estimates in mind, and export the experimental layout. That layout travels far. Power / Design uses it to set sampling assumptions, and later, once the experiment is acquired and measured, Dose–Response uses its dose and condition identities, so keep them unchanged all the way through.

Dose–Response answers how much, not which guide, so it needs no sequencing at all. Open it from Home and bring your measured responses with the dose and condition identities from Experiment Design. Set the dose and response columns, controls and units, then fit the curves. It saves assay results with figures and tables to export.

Once you have more than one analysis, open Run Compare from Home. It reads your saved run records and Regression results and sets their settings, counts and hit lists side by side. If the input data changed between runs, the differences are not a controlled model comparison, so read them with that in mind.

One more planning tool lives only in Python: the pooled-screen simulation sweep, spacr.sim.run_multiple_simulations, with no Home tile or menu entry. You give it a settings dictionary of assumptions, such as screen size, occupancy, classifier accuracy and sequencing. It expands every combination, simulates each in a process pool and appends synthetic summary rows to simulations.db; the call itself returns None. Keep the parameter grid small and set max_workers explicitly before you run it. What comes out is planning evidence, not data, and it cannot stand in for measurements or barcode counts in Regression. Read the summaries, record your assumptions, and carry them by hand into Power / Design or Experiment Design, since neither tool imports the simulation database.

So the barcode side of a screen always ends the same way: identities joined to phenotypes by plate and well. Keep barcode references and plate layouts with your count tables, and for an optical screen, join the decoded objects to their phenotypes and aggregate them before Regression. The linked module lessons show the settings and outputs for each step.
